sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Ramaria formosa forms a branched coral-like bush, generally 7–20 cm wide and 7–20 cm high. Its branches are salmon-pink to whitish, with lemon-yellow tips in young specimens; the tips fade with age. The base is thick and whitish.

sections.title: Cut surface and useful characters
sections.text: The flesh is white to pinkish and may turn brown or black after injury. The fungus has no visible gills or pores; the hymenium covers the branch surfaces. The spore deposit is ochre-yellow. Odour is not a consistent character, and reports of taste vary.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This fungus grows on the ground in broad-leaved woods, especially under beech and oak, often on calcareous soil. It appears mainly in late summer and autumn.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: Other pink or yellow ramarias may look similar; identifying a branched coral requires checking its base, colours and habitat, and sometimes microscopic characters. Ramaria formosa is toxic and can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Do not eat it.

traits: Coral-like bush generally 7–20 cm wide and high, on a thick whitish base

safetyNote: Toxic: may cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Do not eat it. Removing the tips does not make the mushroom safe.
